messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Stan github member

On Tuesday, May 14, 2013 8:08:29 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> But I don't think our problems are that strongly related to not using pull requests. We just have poor workflow.

Could you elaborate on what you think a better workflow would be?
Ideally in terms I can understand that don't involve page after
page of Git diagrams?  If not, I can try to get through something
more involved over the next few days.  But I really don't understand
all of these pages of git instructions.

I think it is probably at least as important that we all standardize on a workflow as it is to debate the merits of the multiple workflows supported by git / github / gerrit / etc. But here are a bunch of things I think

-- If a project has good tests, then that mitigates a lot of problems. But:

---- Our test suite has grown so big that it is not feasible for everyone to run on every commit
---- There are still things that are not easily caught by the unit tests
---- There are some things that pass test-unit with whatever toolchain the author is using but not some other toolchain

To overcome this somewhat, I've emailed to see if we can push to a repository on Hotfoot that would run test-unit in about 2 minutes. That would make it feasible to test every commit and only use the Windows box that Jenkins is on for batches of commits that may be ready for master.

-- Our commits are not good.

---- The commit messages are often not that informative
---- The commits lump together things that should be separate commits
---- Separate commits are used for things that should be lumped together (like "made change, will test and document later")
---- Stuff gets committed that doesn't compile. Note that this is a "git commit" issue rather than a "git push" or "git pull" issue. In other words, this is bad:

Commit A: Add feature, fix bug, whatever
Commit B: Oops, made mistake that broke compilation, now fixed

If you push both of these commits, then (among other reasons) if there is a need to "git bisect" the tree to fix some subtle problem and the bisection lands on Commit B, then git can't tell whether Commit B is good or bad with respect to the subtle problem under investigation because it just terminates in a compiler error. This happened most recently with the different numerical results between g++ (!Windows) and mingw64; I couldn't get to the first commit that exacerbated the numerical differences because it was somewhere in a sequence of about 20 commits that didn't even compile.

The thing to do is either use the --amend flag to "git commit" when committing B to the history, which doesn't actually commit B to the history but instead changes Commit A so that it incorporates the change induced by Commit B and thus (for historical purposes) never breaks the build. Or if you discover that Commit A was faulty after already making some intermediate commits, you can use "git rebase -i" to squash Commit A and Commit B into a single commit (say Commit AB) before pushing anywhere (and thereby making the history essentially irrevocable). If we do that, then "git bisect" often locates the root of the problem quickly and essentially automatically.

-- Stuff is going into master way too soon

--- Where it should go depends on a project's workflow, but there is never a rush to go into master and master should always be usable. In other words, anyone should be able to clone the master branch on GitHub and get a working Stan or RStan so we have to be careful about when and what gets merged into master.
--- Branches are so cheap in git and so easy to work with in GitHub that nothing is lost by saying "I've pushed some stuff into branch foo. Can people test it / comment on it and we'll see about merging it into master later?" We had such a branch with the hmc_refactor thing, but it got merged into master before there was time to figure out all the issues that a change of that magnitude would raise.

-- I don't think pull requests are all that great for Stan in general

---- There are a qualified blessing for outside contributors that happen to have GitHub accounts
---- They are a nuisance if the pull request is just something like "I eliminated some already completed cruft off the TO-DO list"
---- Having someone else give approval is overkill if the pull request is something like "I added a test that passes". 99% of the time there is going to be no objection and the 1% of the time that the test is actually flawed is not worth the hassle of going through the pull request
---- If something merits a pull request, it probably merits a group discussion and testing with multiple toolchains, as opposed to one person approving the pull request. This is because Stan is complicated and most people don't know that much about certain parts of it. In other words, I would favor a process where bigger changes are discussed and tested, objections are resolved, and when there are no more objections, someone pushes it to master.

-- I've never used gitflow myself, but it is widely used and seems to help with discipline

---- There is the master branch and the development branch (among others)
---- New features get pushed to the development branch before they are pushed to the master branch. In other words, the development branch is somewhat like how we have been using the master branch thusfar
---- There are also hotfix branches that fix bugs but do not add new features. A hotfix branch is merged into both the development branch and the master branch.
---- Whenever the master branch changes, you (can) do a release

You probably want some degree of human review before something goes into development (at least if it touches stan/src) and definitely want human review before it goes into master. But you don't want too high of a hurdle for a push to some feature branch that maybe multiple people are working on before it gets pushed to the development branch.

Git is complicated, but it is now beating every other version control system for open source projects, including ones that are bigger or more complicated than Stan. Few projects move away from git and many are moving to it, which causes temporary headaches for people learning the ropes. But we've been using git for a long time now, and it shouldn't be beyond our capability to use it well.

Ben

0. Fork the stan-dev/stan repository to a personal repository.
1. Update the personal/stan master repository.
2. Make changes (either to personal/stan/master or personal/stan/branch).
3. Update master, merge master into current branch (if branch==master, that's fine). Test as much needs to be tested locally.
4. Create a pull request.

For a new feature, bug fix, or anything else, start at 1.

For the pull request:
1. Someone informally code review it and declare it to be ok.
1. Start the build on Jenkins (instructions to come).
3. One of the persons with "pull & push" access merge into master and push the changes.

I think it is probably at least as important that we all standardize on a workflow as it is to debate the merits of the
multiple workflows supported by git / github / gerrit / etc. But here are a bunch of things I think

-- If a project has good tests, then that mitigates a lot of problems. But:

---- Our test suite has grown so big that it is not feasible for everyone to run on every commit
---- There are still things that are not easily caught by the unit tests
---- There are some things that pass test-unit with whatever toolchain the author is using but not some other toolchain

To overcome this somewhat, I've emailed to see if we can push to a repository on Hotfoot that would run test-unit in
about 2 minutes. That would make it feasible to test every commit and only use the Windows box that Jenkins is on for
batches of commits that may be ready for master.

-- Our commits are not good.

---- The commit messages are often not that informative
---- The commits lump together things that should be separate commits
---- Separate commits are used for things that should be lumped together (like "made change, will test and document later")
---- Stuff gets committed that doesn't compile. Note that this is a "git commit" issue rather than a "git push" or "git
pull" issue. In other words, this is bad:

Commit A: Add feature, fix bug, whatever
Commit B: Oops, made mistake that broke compilation, now fixed

If you push both of these commits, then (among other reasons) if there is a need to "git bisect" the tree to fix some
subtle problem and the bisection lands on Commit B, then git can't tell whether Commit B is good or bad with respect to
the subtle problem under investigation because it just terminates in a compiler error. This happened most recently with
the different numerical results between g++ (!Windows) and mingw64; I couldn't get to the first commit that exacerbated
the numerical differences because it was somewhere in a sequence of about 20 commits that didn't even compile.

The thing to do is either use the --amend flag to "git commit" when committing B to the history, which doesn't actually
commit B to the history but instead changes Commit A so that it incorporates the change induced by Commit B and thus
(for historical purposes) never breaks the build. Or if you discover that Commit A was faulty after already making some
intermediate commits, you can use "git rebase -i" to squash Commit A and Commit B into a single commit (say Commit AB)
before pushing anywhere (and thereby making the history essentially irrevocable). If we do that, then "git bisect" often
locates the root of the problem quickly and essentially automatically.

-- Stuff is going into master way too soon

--- Where it should go depends on a project's workflow, but there is never a rush to go into master and master should
always be usable. In other words, anyone should be able to clone the master branch on GitHub and get a working Stan or
RStan so we have to be careful about when and what gets merged into master.
--- Branches are so cheap in git and so easy to work with in GitHub that nothing is lost by saying "I've pushed some
stuff into branch foo. Can people test it / comment on it and we'll see about merging it into master later?" We had such
a branch with the hmc_refactor thing, but it got merged into master before there was time to figure out all the issues
that a change of that magnitude would raise.

-- I don't think pull requests are all that great for Stan in general

---- There are a qualified blessing for outside contributors that happen to have GitHub accounts
---- They are a nuisance if the pull request is just something like "I eliminated some already completed cruft off the
TO-DO list"
---- Having someone else give approval is overkill if the pull request is something like "I added a test that passes".
99% of the time there is going to be no objection and the 1% of the time that the test is actually flawed is not worth
the hassle of going through the pull request
---- If something merits a pull request, it probably merits a group discussion and testing with multiple toolchains, as
opposed to one person approving the pull request. This is because Stan is complicated and most people don't know that
much about certain parts of it. In other words, I would favor a process where bigger changes are discussed and tested,
objections are resolved, and when there are no more objections, someone pushes it to master.

-- I've never used gitflow myself, but it is widely used and seems to help with discipline

---- There is the master branch and the development branch (among others)
---- New features get pushed to the development branch before they are pushed to the master branch. In other words, the
development branch is somewhat like how we have been using the master branch thusfar
---- There are also hotfix branches that fix bugs but do not add new features. A hotfix branch is merged into both the
development branch and the master branch.
---- Whenever the master branch changes, you (can) do a release

You probably want some degree of human review before something goes into development (at least if it touches stan/src)
and definitely want human review before it goes into master. But you don't want too high of a hurdle for a push to some
feature branch that maybe multiple people are working on before it gets pushed to the development branch.

Git is complicated, but it is now beating every other version control system for open source projects, including ones
that are bigger or more complicated than Stan. Few projects move away from git and many are moving to it, which causes
temporary headaches for people learning the ropes. But we've been using git for a long time now, and it shouldn't be
beyond our capability to use it well.

Ben

A hotfix branch would often just have one commit and is merged into both the development branch and the master branch (at which point you could do a release if the bug were severe enough). For what it is worth, a feature branch would regularly git pull from the development branch as the feature is being developed and thus would get the hotfixes as they arise.

this would probably entail a nonminimal bump of the version number

So, you can implement a feature in a feature branch and rewrite your history before merging it into the development branch. But it is easier to get things right the first time ...

So, you can implement a feature in a feature branch and rewrite your history before merging it into the development branch

How to rewrite history? git rebase?

Mostly, yes. Or if you just need to rewrite the previous commit, then

git commit --amend

Or, if

git rebase -i

is not what you want, you can do

git diff development > /tmp/big_patch.diff
git checkout development
git branch -D feature
git branch feature
git checkout feature
git apply /tmp/big_patch.diff

and then add and commit appropriate chunks of your big_patch as the new history.

The main thing is to not rewrite history if someone else has already branched from some point in the old history because then they can't merge. So, you can only change the history of local branches and possibly public feature branches (because feature branches should generally branch directly from the development branch).

Ben

Just so everyone is clear, we're really talking about two different
things here. They're related and both of them should be addressed,
but they are distinct.

1. The gitflow discussion relates to how we manage releases and the
main Stan repository. What goes where, when and in what state. What
do different branches mean, when do they merge, and in what direction,
etc. In other words, how all of us work jointly on Stan.

2. The commit history discussion relates to how we work locally.
Ideally every commit should build and, hopefully, pass unit tests. I
think that's a good goal to keep in mind but a little overly
optimistic, and perhaps even a little counter intuitive because it
will lead to Balkanization of commits. I.E., instead of committing
often with small changes, this encourages large block commits which
have been fully vetted and makes git bisect similarly useless. (If it
comes down to a single commit, but that commit touches dozens of files
and changes hundreds of lines of code, that's not terribly helpful.)

For 1) I like the gitflow process, it seems to makes sense, and
ensures that we can always do a release with a bug fix if needed.

For 2) I see Ben has already posted something, but roughly speaking,
it means before we do a git push, we should do a git rebase -i and
clean up our commits. It's also probably a good idea to do the git
rebase regularly for longer lasting feature branches to keep your
history clean since doing a rebase at the end of a long development
cycle can be painful and require a lot of manual merging.

Cheers,

This is *exactly* what I worry about with doing everything through
pull requests. There are many many commits which are small and
obvious and do not need a full process of review/compile/test. If we
make even these commits hard or time-consuming to do, they won't
happen at all or will instead get folded into much larger pull
requests whose correctness aren't at all obvious.

If we're going to require *every* commit to compile and pass unit
tests then we need some a bigger testing infrastructure (i.e., servers
which test every commit in every pull request, automatically and,
ideally, quickly) to do this and it needs to be smooth and painless.
I'm not convinced this is possible with GitHub's pull request
framework, as it seems to struggle with anything other than an
immediate merge. E.G., if one commit in a large sequence breaks
tests, this is going to require a rebase and a whole new pull request
which is not only tedious, but looses the whole thread of discussion
in the issue tracker.

I really think the solution here is that we all just try to be better
about our workflows and try to make things clean when we do push.
That, combined with a disciplined version of something like gitflow,
should make things much smoother going forward.

Cheers,
Marcus

A rebase attempts to replay some or all of your commits as if they
were applied starting from a different point. Sometimes that doesn't
happen cleanly because of conflicts. Think of a rebase like this:

Imagine you have a sequence of 10 commits. Commit 1 was originally
off of the HEAD of master, but there was another commit on master, so
it has a new HEAD and you want commits 1 through 10 to look as if they
happened on this new HEAD and you'd like to combine or reorder some of
them to make things look nicer.

To do this, git rebase creates a sequence of patches from your 10
commits, goes to the new head that you're trying to rebase onto and
then tries to replay these patches on this new head, one at a time, to
create a new set of commits. There can often be conflicts in this
process.

> A rebase attempts to replay some or all of your commits as if they

My question is what happens to bisect when run on dev.
I thought we wound up with something like this:

   DEV:  a ---------------> b
           \                ^
            \              /
BRANCH      c ---> d --> e


but with fast forward, we get:

          a -> c -> d -> e

When we bisect on DEV in the first case, does it only consider
a and b, or does it also look at c, d, and e?

git bisect is a commit level concept rather than a branch concept, so it should drill down to the first bad commit in the history between the bracket commits. Although, git bisect would require fewer tests to find the first bad commit if there were a nice simple history between the brackets, it will find it eventually as long as all the commits can definitively test for the problem (as opposed to bombing because of a missing semicolon in a commit)

I was sort of hoping that the bisect on dev would find which branch
introduced the problem, then bisecting that branch would find the commit.
No, it just finds the commit.

> As a rule (without extreme pain) we can't rebase anything that has
> landed into dev, master or any other branch that we expect people to
> branch off of.  Rebase rewrites history in a way that breaks anyone
> who branched from that history.

I thought the idea was to rebase the branch before merging it.

No one should rebase something that someone else could reasonably have branched from (due to the impossibility of merging later). So, you can't rebase the development branch before branching a release branch from it since people will have branched from development to make a feature branch. That person can usually rebase a feature branch before it is merged into the development branch.

I've only thought about this through bisect --- are there other implications?
I'm not sure what "rewrites history" means here.  (Or what Ben meant about
backing out features creating a circular history.)

The main implication is the ability to merge rather than the ability to bisect. There are a couple of other ways to rewrite history that I mentioned to Mav, namely git commit --amend and making a patch, applying that patch to a new branch, and adding / committing chunks at a time.
